Article Title: In 1940, Nazis seized a 3-inch painting from a Jewish collector in Vienna; 86 years later, Austria returned it to his heir in Minnesota
Article Text:
Return to the heirs

An 1847 painting made by a not-so-popular artist wouldn't have much historical or monetary value for most. But to Jackie Sondell, whose three grandparents died in the Holocaust, it's a priceless family heirloom. The Austrian deputy consul general in the Twin Cities, from his posting in New York, lifted the top off a cardboard box and pulled out a tiny piece of art. The 1847 watercolour miniature, about 3 inches tall and 2 inches wide, showed a nobleman who was an officer in the Austrian Empire's army and was stolen from the house of Sondell's relative Eduard Epstein in Vienna, Austria, by the Nazis, as per a report by The Minnesota Star Tribune.It was painted by Albert Theer, an Austrian painter not much famed in history. For years, the miniature had been overlooked at the Museum of Military History in Vienna. Then, the Austrian diplomat handed over the painting to its rightful heir, Jackie Sondell, a retired real estate agent who lived in Wayzata. “I see it as a symbol of hope,” Sondell said.The Austrian government had tracked down the 77-year-old Sondell and her brother, Jeff Lieb, after officials learned the siblings were the heirs of Eduard Epstein.Epstein had been a successful Jewish merchant in the Viennese textile industry in the early 1900s and an enthusiastic art collector.But when the Nazis took control of Austria in 1938, Epstein's circumstances changed dramatically. His company was liquidated, and his valuables including jewellery, coin collections, and silver were requisitioned. When he tried to sell his art collection to fund an escape from the widening terror of the Nazis, he was caught and sent to prison for 10 months. He finally managed to flee to America in 1941 with his wife and daughter. Weakened by prison, he died two years later at 62. Epstein’s family never saw his art collection again, lost to the Nazis and to history.It was in 2013, when the miniature watercolour of the Austrian nobleman was identified in the Vienna military museum. It was submitted to an art restitution board, part of a broad effort across Austria in recent decades to return art stolen by the Nazis.Tracking down heirs to a painting stolen nearly a century ago can be difficult, explained the Austrian diplomat, Johannes Gassner. But last year a government representative tracked down Sondell and told her about the painting. Growing up, Sondell and her brother were close to their Aunt Helen and Uncle Ernest. Helen was the only daughter of Epstein and his wife, Margarete. Helen was not Sondell's blood relative, but had married into the family when she married Sondell's Uncle Ernest. Since Helen and Ernest didn’t have children, they treated Sondell and her brother like their own, spoiling them with summer trips to the Adirondacks or adventures in New York City. When Helen died in 2000, Sondell and her brother became heirs to her estate.Sondell called Dorotheum, one of the world’s oldest auction houses in Vienna, to learn about the miniature’s history. Researchers told her Epstein had been arrested when he tried to sell the art, which the Nazis seized on March 28, 1940.“Austria took a while to accept responsibility for its role in the crimes and atrocities committed by the Nazi regime,” Gassner said. “Of course you cannot undo what happened, and you cannot restore the lives of all those who were murdered. But nevertheless today’s restitution is an important gesture in the context of Austria’s efforts to live up to its historical responsibility. It’s never too late to accept responsibility. ”As the diplomat travelled to Minnesota to return the painting, Sondell felt emotional. She thought about how her aunt Helen would have felt if she were alive. And how the Holocaust formed a part in her family's history, where she lost three grandparents to it: one in Dachau, two at the Sobibor extermination camp in Poland. “May their memories be a blessing,” Sondell said. Sondell’s mother escaped to London before making her way to the United States, but the Holocaust was never far from her mother’s mind.However belated it was for Austria to recognise its responsibility, Sondell appreciated it. She hopes the return of the painting highlights the individual Jewish lives brutally affected by the Holocaust. Six million Jews dead is a soul-numbing statistic, but Eduard Epstein’s story is a tragedy.“No matter what size the picture is, at least they are making the effort of returning it,” Sondell said. “You have to give somebody a second chance. If you stop and forgive, maybe the world will see things a different way. Maybe there is hope for peace in the world.”Interestingly, the miniature makes up just one piece of Epstein's large art collection. The whereabouts of the rest of his art still remain unknown with no full accounting of what was stolen.
Article Summary: Jackie Sondell's relative Eduard Epstein's art collection was stolen by the Nazis in 1940. Epstein was arrested when he tried to sell his art collection to fund an escape from the widening terror of the Nazis. He finally managed to flee to America in 1941 with his wife and daughter. The miniature had been overlooked at the Museum of Military History in Vienna for years.

Article Title: Germany blames Russia for drone attack attempt at Leipzig/Halle airport
Article Text:
A police drone checks an aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport, where a drone with an explosive device was found in Germany. (Photo: AP)

Germany blames Russia for Leipzig/Halle drone attempt

Berlin closes Russian consulate, tightens restrictions

Moscow rejects allegation, warns of response

Two grid attacks investigated separately

Rockets cause two short circuits in Brandenburg

Germany-Russia tensions escalated on Tuesday after Berlin formally blamed Moscow for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport and announced a series of diplomatic and security measures, as police separately investigated two suspected attacks on Germany's electricity network within hours of each other.German authorities have not linked either grid incident to Russia or to the Leipzig/Halle case. Police have also not established whether the two electricity-network attacks were connected.Berlin said Russia was responsible for an attempted attack involving an explosives-laden drone found near Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport on August 4.Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said police findings, intelligence and the pattern of the operation pointed to people acting on behalf of Russian state agencies. He said the drone configuration, components, explosives and ignition systems were known from other Russian hybrid operations and Russia's war against Ukraine.Leipzig/Halle is a major freight hub and also handles logistics linked to military support for Ukraine.Germany responded by ordering Russia's Consulate General in Bonn to close from September 18 and ending the lease for the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin.The government also plans to seek new EU listings of Russian individuals linked to hybrid attacks, tighten immigration controls on Russian nationals, increase pressure on Russia's shadow fleet and take further measures in the intelligence sector. Germany also summoned the Russian ambassador, the Federal Foreign Office said.Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany would continue its civilian and military support for Ukraine and work with NATO and European Union partners to strengthen defences against hybrid threats.Several European governments backed Germany. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she would discuss the attack with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, while EU foreign ministers were preparing a joint response.Russia rejected Germany's accusation and accused Berlin of further damaging already strained relations.The Russian embassy in Germany called the allegation baseless and described Berlin's measures as an "unprecedented escalation" that would have consequences.Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said Moscow would respond, while Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Germany had not presented evidence to substantiate its accusation.President Vladimir Putin also questioned Berlin's evidence and accused Germany of planting evidence to frame Russia. He claimed Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government was using the case to divert attention from domestic problems and falling approval ratings, but provided no evidence for either allegation.German police are separately investigating two suspected deliberate attacks on electricity infrastructure that occurred within hours of each other on Tuesday.A short circuit at an Amprion substation in Bergheim-Rheidt in western Germany on Tuesday evening put several power lines out of service without disrupting electricity supplies to households.Police were alerted at around 1800 GMT and believe the short circuit was deliberately caused rather than the result of a technical fault, German public broadcaster WDR reported, citing an Essen police spokesperson.Police have not said what caused the short circuit or whether any device was used. Investigators are examining whether the incident could be connected to an attack earlier that day in Brandenburg, but no link has been established.Hours earlier, projectiles carrying conductive material struck extra-high-voltage lines near the Turnow-Preilack substation in Brandenburg, causing two short circuits.The attack briefly interrupted power and automatically shut down one unit at the Jänschwalde power plant. Operator LEAG expected the unit to return to service by Tuesday evening, while transmission operator 50Hertz said the affected lines had been restored and the wider electricity supply was not disrupted.Investigators found a double-digit number of devices at the site, some of which had not activated. Police secured evidence and appealed for witnesses who may have seen the attack or possible suspects on Tuesday morning.The Turnow-Preilack substation is a key high-voltage node linking Jänschwalde, Brandenburg's largest power plant, to the 50Hertz transmission network.Brandenburg Interior Minister Jan Redmann said the devices had been specially constructed and were unlike ordinary fireworks, with their preparation requiring significant work. He did not rule out involvement by a foreign power or left-wing activists.Investigators have not attributed the Brandenburg attack to any state or group and are still trying to establish whether it was connected to the later incident in Bergheim.
Article Summary: Berlin blames Russia for attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport. Russia rejects allegation, warns of response. Two grid attacks investigated separately in Brandenburg and Bergheim-Rheidt. Police have not linked either grid incident to Russia or to the case.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Li Ka-shing: "You can believe in Fung Shui if you want, but ultimately people control…" - a timeless lesson on effort and self-improvement
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Li Ka-shing (AP photo)

Quote of the day by Li Ka-shing

"You can believe in Fung Shui if you want, but ultimately people control their own fate"

The wisdom hidden in Li Ka-shing’s quote

What "ultimately people control their own fate" genuinely means

Why this quote genuinely still matters today

Focus on what is genuinely within your control

Improvement rarely happens all at once

Effort becomes considerably more useful once it is properly directed

Do not let someone else's progress genuinely define your own

Other memorable quotes by Li Ka-shing

"Vision is perhaps our greatest strength. It has kept us alive to the power and continuity of thought through the centuries, it makes us peer into the future and lends shape to the unknown."

"Broaden your vision, and maintain stability while advancing forward. That is my philosophy."

"It doesn't matter how strong or capable you are; if you don't have a big heart, you will not succeed."

"A good reputation for yourself and your company is an invaluable asset not reflected in the balance sheets."

How to apply Li Ka-shing’s quote in daily life

Final takeaway from the quote by Li Ka-shing

There are moments when people quietly blame circumstances for the way things turn out. Luck, timing, family background, money and simple chance can all appear to have a genuine say in where a person actually ends up. Li Ka-shing, the Hong Kong businessman and philanthropist, took a genuinely different view of this. "You can believe in Fung Shui if you want, but ultimately people control their own fate," he said. "The most important thing is to improve yourself and give it your best. Then many things previously thought to be impossible will become possible." This line is extremely widely and consistently repeated across dozens of independent collections of his sayings, with no disputes or competing versions anywhere, though no single dated interview or speech could be pinned down as its original source. Li himself became one of Asia's most prominent entrepreneurs after genuinely starting out with very little, which gives the quote real weight beyond a simple motivational line.The quote opens with a reference to Fung Shui, but its actual central message is not really about whether a person believes in it at all. Li shifts the focus deliberately away from external forces and toward genuine personal effort instead.Whatever someone actually believes about luck or fate, there are still real things within their own control. Skills can genuinely be developed. Knowledge can actually be gained. A mistake can honestly be examined. None of this means every person genuinely starts from the same position, or that hard work alone guarantees a particular outcome. Circumstances genuinely matter, and opportunity is never distributed equally. The real point is considerably narrower and more practical than that. A person cannot control everything that happens to them, but they can genuinely influence how they prepare, respond and continue afterward.This phrase is easy to misread if taken to mean people have complete control over their entire life. They genuinely do not. Nobody actually chooses the circumstances they are born into, and nobody can control an economic downturn, an illness, or an unexpected accident. What people can very often control is what they actually do with the circumstances genuinely in front of them. Someone lacking a particular skill can learn it. Someone who performs poorly can honestly examine what actually went wrong. These actions never guarantee success. They do, though, genuinely change what possibilities remain actually available to a person going forward.Modern life gives people considerably more visibility into other people's success than ever before. On social media, it is genuinely easy to see someone announce a promotion or launch a business. What usually stays missing is everything that actually happened before that announcement, the years of real preparation, the failed attempts, and the ordinary days when nothing seemed to be changing at all. That can make success look like pure luck. Li's quote offers a genuinely different way to look at real progress. Rather than spending time trying to understand why someone else appears further ahead, attention can be brought back to what can genuinely still be improved.There will always be real circumstances that cannot actually be changed. Spending all of your energy fighting those circumstances can leave very little attention left for the decisions that are genuinely still available to you. The genuinely useful question is often not why something happened to you, but what you can actually do from here.People sometimes expect real, visible progress fairly quickly, and when it does not appear, they assume their effort simply is not working. Improvement can genuinely be difficult to notice while it is actually happening. A person may learn something new or make fewer mistakes without seeing one single dramatic change. Small gains genuinely accumulate over time.Simply working longer never automatically produces better results on its own. A person may spend genuine hours studying without actually understanding the subject properly. Giving something your genuine best also involves paying real attention to what is actually working, and honestly changing whatever is not.Comparison can make real personal improvement considerably harder to actually notice. Someone else may genuinely be moving faster for reasons that have very little to do with your own actual circumstances. The more genuinely useful comparison is very often simply with where you actually were before.The most genuinely practical part of Li Ka-shing's observation is the actual instruction to improve yourself, and that can begin with something quite ordinary. Someone who genuinely wants to move into a new career can spend real time learning the skills required for it, rather than simply waiting for the perfect opportunity to arrive. A student who genuinely finds a subject difficult can identify the specific areas actually causing trouble, instead of simply deciding they are "bad" at the whole thing entirely. The same principle genuinely works outside work and education too. A person trying to become more organised can start by changing just one routine. None of this promises a particular result. What it does is genuinely increase a person's actual ability to respond once circumstances genuinely change.Li Ka-shing's quote does not suggest that life sits entirely within an individual's own control. It makes a considerably more measured point than that. There will always be things people genuinely cannot predict or change. There will also always be real decisions they can make, real skills they can develop, and genuine habits they can improve. Fate may decide where a person actually starts, and circumstances may genuinely influence the road ahead. Preparation, though, can decide how ready someone actually is for the next opportunity that comes along. Sometimes the biggest genuine change is never really in the situation itself. It is in the person actually facing it.
Article Summary: "ultimately people control their own fate" is the quote of the day by Li Ka- shing. The Hong Kong businessman and philanthropist took a genuinely different view of this. Li himself became one of Asia's most prominent entrepreneurs after genuinely starting out with little.

Article Title: New England has battled invasive green crabs for more than 200 years; now people are eating the destructive species in a bid to protect shellfish, wetlands and coastal ecosystems
Article Text:
An invasive species

Climate change on their side

Crab fisheries on the rise?

Green crab on the menu

Since time immemorial, humans have been consuming food derived from the land, air and water. From vegetables and birds to even crabs, there is not much we have not used to survive on. But currently, people in New England are feasting on green crabs not to survive themselves but to help the native species subsist. Every morning in Maine's York River, fishers look for the region's most despised crabs and find few that end up on someone's plate, according to a report by AP.The trick is to identify invasive European green crabs that are about to shed their hard shell or moult, revealing a softer exterior that has the feel of a leather couch and is in demand at restaurants. Not only do these crabs fetch more money, $3 per crab at the market, but catching them is also doing a service for the ocean's ecosystem. “Just about everyone hates them, and we’re trying to turn them into a premium seafood product,” said Mike Masi, whose company, shell+claw, is the only one that commercially cultivates these crabs.Masi, a 45-year-old former marine science teacher is a part of the growing movement across New England aiming to lessen the crabs' destructive impact by developing new markets.Others are putting green crabs in pet treats, fish sauce and even a line of green crab whiskey in New Hampshire.The green crabs, Carcinus maenus, made their way from Europe to the East Coast on ships centuries ago. Now numbering in tens of millions, they outcompete Atlantic rock crab and juvenile lobster, destroy eelgrass beds and undermine salt marsh banks. They also are costing the region’s shellfish industry tens of millions of dollars each year, as they eat mussels, oysters and soft-shell clams.Chad Coffin, a clam fisherman from Maine, blamed the emergence of green crabs for the decline of his catch. Soft-shell clam landings have gone from over 7.8 million meat pounds (3.6 million kilograms) in 1978 to 1.3 million pounds (572,644 kilograms) in 2025, according to the state.Green crabs are known for their brown or green shells and five spines on either side of their eyes. The warming of the ocean waters due to global warming and climate change has been helpful for their population. The crabs are able to survive New England winters while also thriving in a range of diverse habitats. They eat almost anything and produce plenty of young; a female will release up to 185,000 eggs once or twice a year.These traits have made them among the world’s most successful invasive species, expanding along the West Coast and into Alaska and reaching South Africa, Japan, Argentina and Australia.“They’re really pretty resilient little guys,” said Carolyn Tepolt, an evolutionary biologist at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution who has studied green crabs for two decades and uses them to understand why some species thrive in different environments.For the past decade, the region's campaign to combat the crab invasion has been limited to the grassroots, causing not much impact on their numbers. While a growing number of restaurants and seafood businesses are now offering green crabs, very few New England fishermen are catching them, and there is almost no infrastructure to process the catch and get them to market.Marissa McMahan, vice president of fisheries at Manomet Conservation Sciences, says that people in Washington County, Maine, on the Canadian border, tell her they can catch “as many green crabs as you could ever possibly want.” “But they can’t get them on a truck and get them to where they need to actually be, and often that’s Boston or New Bedford or New York City,” she said. “That is a huge impediment.”Certain steps have been taken in the right direction. Rhode Island passed a law that offers a green crab fishing license for just $10, Connecticut now allows crabs to be sold as food and Maine has made it easier to get the crabs to the market.The problem, many advocates say, is the absence of significant government support in New England. Only Massachusetts offers incentives to catch them: Fishermen receive 40 cents per pound on top of what they get selling them, or just over $100,000 per year in state funding. The state program operates in 10 communities on the North Shore and outer Cape Cod.Meanwhile, Washington state declared an emergency in 2022 and expects to spend more than $38 million in state and federal funds through fiscal year 2027 eradicating the crabs. So far this year, nearly 2 million crabs have been caught and mostly converted into 135,000 pounds (61,234 kilograms) of waste that goes to an organic fertiliser company. The Shoalwater Bay Indian Tribe and Lummi Nation also catch crabs and use them as compost.According to the report by AP, there is a rising appetite for green crabs in New England. Since 2021, advocates have observed a more than 10-fold increase in restaurants offering crab. Some are putting fried green crab in sandwiches, on top of pasta dishes and in their sauces. Many take part in green crab weeks that happen during the roughly two-month softshell season. PAGU, a Spanish Japanese tapas restaurant in Cambridge, Massachusetts, puts the crustaceans into the broth of its green crab laksa, a Malaysian-inspired noodle soup, and, when available, puts a tempura-fried soft-shell green crab inside a steamed bun called bao. “These crabs are way more potent in terms of flavour,” said PAGU’s chef and owner Tracy Chang.The industrial-scale green crabbing is a long way off, according to Masi. While his business has grown since he began five years ago, he says it still feels like a hobby that brings in up to $20,000 annually. Yet he remains "cautiously optimistic" about the potential of this business. And the hope might be right as long as people keep on loving the flavours of the green crabs along with their health benefits.
Article Summary: Green crabs are known for their brown or green shells and five spines on either side of their eyes. The warming of the ocean waters due to global warming and climate change has been helpful for their population. The crabs are able to survive New England winters while also thriving in a range of diverse habitats. They eat almost anything and produce plenty of young.

Article Title: Meet Mike Nithavrianakis, former British diplomat to Pakistan who is running a global marathon to help educate 25.2 million children in the country
Article Text: Mike Nithavrianakis worked as a British diplomat in Pakistan for three years from 2019 to 2022, working as Deputy High Commissioner in Karachi and Trade Director for Pakistan. During his time there, he clearly remembers his first visit to a school run by The Citizens Foundation (TCF) in Pakistan, The students in the classrooms were intrigued by their lessons and displayed what he described to IBT as a genuine "thirst for learning and knowledge. " Not just the students, the staff welcomed him warmly, the head teacher was humble and deeply committed to the school she led.The visit revealed to Nithavrianakis the enormous disparities within the country's education system. In a country of enormous size and population, education opportunities range from elite private schools to no schools at all. Today, approximately 25.2 million children in Pakistan remain out of school and Nithavrianakis is working to solve this situation."My first school visit left a deep imprint. I have many lasting impressions, but the clearest memory is of interacting with a group of quite young pupils who were so engrossed that one could literally see their thirst for learning and knowledge," he said to the outlet. That encounter fostered a long relationship with TCF. During his three years in Pakistan, he asked TCF co-founder Mushtaq Chhapra how he could help. Chhapra encouraged him to spread the word about the organisation and its mission.But he wanted to do something even more impactful and his hobby of running offered an answer. "I wanted to do more than that and thought combining my passion for running with fundraising for TCF would be a small gesture of support."During his diplomatic posting, he took on the London and Manchester marathons within a week of each other to raise money for the foundation, generating more than $350,000. This helped fund a new TCF campus in Matiari District, Sindh, leading to its name, TCH School, The Nithavrianakis Campus.Now, he has extended the scale of his efforts. Through the 2026 Global Run for Education, he aims to raise $1 million for TCF. Based on the organisation's annual cost of educating one student, that amount is equivalent to supporting roughly 6,000 students for a full academic year.His 2026 race schedule includes Milan on April 12, London on April 26, Sydney on August 30, Chicago on October 11 and New York City on November 1, before culminating in Karachi on January 3, 2027. Additional race entries may be announced as plans are finalised.TCF currently operates 2,261 school units serving 320,000 students across Pakistan. Its 16,500 teachers are women, and the organisation maintains a commitment to balanced enrollment among girls and boys. Its schools are designed to make education more accessible in underserved communities, including for families who might otherwise struggle to send their children to school. Nithavrianakis hopes the campaign can extend TCF's educational opportunities to more children. "I sincerely hope that it gives them the best possible chance to benefit from a fantastic education and maximise their potential. All any parent can hope for in life is that their child is given the same opportunities as others. With TCF, the sky's the limit."Given the strong support for TCF in the United States, Nithavrianakis is also considering how future race entries could help reach new supporters in 2027 and beyond.As a career diplomat, Nithavrianakis has had eight substantive postings with the UK Foreign Service, including Malaysia, Russia, Ghana, Saudi Arabia, India, Pakistan and Somalia. He recently retired from the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO). "Speaking from the heart, there is no better feeling than seeking support for a cause like TCF. I have realised in later life that giving is so much more rewarding and enjoyable than receiving," he said.
Article Summary: Mike Nithavrianakis worked as a British diplomat in Pakistan for three years from 2019 to 2022. During his time there, he visited a school run by The Citizens Foundation (TCF) In a country of enormous size and population, education opportunities range from elite private schools to no schools at all. Today, approximately 25.2 million children in Pakistan remain out of school.

Article Title: A Minnesota woman paid $500 to overnight a box she said held cookbooks; a shipping worker opened it with police and found $30,000 in cash meant for scammers
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Suspicious shipping request

Police uncover cash

Woman gets money back

A timely intervention

What looked like an ordinary overnight shipment turned into a scam intervention after a Minnesota shipping company worker became suspicious of a woman's unusually urgent request. The woman had arrived at Graphic Mailbox in Northfield, Minnesota, last week hoping to send a package to Texas. She was prepared to pay $500 for overnight delivery and told staff that the box contained cookbooks. But her behaviour raised questions, and an employee's decision to take a closer look ultimately helped prevent her from losing $30,000. According to CBS Minnesota, which reported the incident, the shipping employee involved noticed that the woman appeared frantic and seemed to have rehearsed answers to questions about the package. When the employee's manager and police became involved, the box was opened and its contents revealed a large amount of cash. The woman had been convinced by scammers to send the money to strangers.The incident began when the woman walked into Graphic Mailbox in Northfield with a package she wanted to send to Texas. According to CBS Minnesota, Graphic Mailbox employee Alice Castro immediately noticed that something seemed unusual.The woman appeared frantic and gave very specific answers to questions, almost as though she had prepared them in advance. Another detail also stood out. The woman was willing to spend $500 to have the package delivered overnight. She told the staff that the box contained cookbooks. However, the combination of her behaviour, the urgency of the shipment and the large amount she was paying for delivery prompted the employee to become concerned. Rather than simply processing the shipment, Castro and her manager, Terri Sim, became involved.The situation took a more serious turn when police were contacted and the package was examined. Inside the box were not cookbooks, but $30,000 in cash. The money was being sent to people the woman did not personally know. She had been instructed to send the cash after scammers convinced her that there was a problem with her financial accounts. Sim told CBS Minnesota that the woman said she had been told her accounts were hacked. The woman also reportedly acknowledged that she had never fallen for this kind of scam before, but said the people contacting her had been convincing. The discovery meant that the package never left the shipping facility.Because the shipment was stopped before it reached its destination, the woman was able to recover the money. She also received a refund of the $500 overnight shipping fee she had paid. For Sim, the episode was more than simply stopping a suspicious package. She told CBS Minnesota that after realising what had happened, she walked around the counter, hugged the woman and reassured her that everything would be okay. The incident highlights how scammers can pressure people into making decisions they might otherwise question. Rather than directly asking victims to hand over money in person, criminals may convince them to withdraw large amounts of cash and send it through shipping services.The incident serves as a reminder that scams can be convincing enough to make otherwise unusual requests seem reasonable. In this case, a simple decision by a shipping employee to ask questions created an opportunity to uncover what was really happening. The intervention also highlights the value of paying attention to warning signs, particularly when a transaction involves unusual urgency or a significant amount of money. By taking the situation seriously rather than treating it as a routine shipment, the employee helped interrupt the scam before it could cause a major financial loss.
Article Summary: The woman arrived at Graphic Mailbox in Northfield, Minnesota, hoping to send a package to Texas. She was prepared to pay $500 for overnight delivery and told staff that the box contained cookbooks. But an employee became suspicious and asked questions about the package. When the employee's manager and police became involved, the box was opened and its contents revealed a large amount of cash. She had been convinced by scammers to send the money to strangers.

Article Title: A Florida family listed its 42.57-acre Clearwater Beach estate for $37.5 million; the state now wants about 28 undeveloped acres to expand Caladesi Island State Park
Article Text:
Clearwater Beach FloridaRepresentative image from Canva

A rare large holding near Clearwater Beach

The $37.5 million listing

The state’s conservation interest

Why this parcel matters for Caladesi Island State Park

The family’s position and community reaction

Funding and the path forward

What’s at stake

On one of the last large, undeveloped stretches of land near Clearwater Beach, a 42.57-acre family estate has sat on the market for $37.5 million, drawing attention from luxury buyers and conservationists alike. Now, the state of Florida has entered the picture, expressing interest in acquiring roughly 28 acres of the property to expand Caladesi Island State Park and protect critical coastal habitat. As reported by AOL and in preliminary evaluations by the Florida Natural Areas Inventory, the potential deal would preserve mangroves, tidal creeks and wildlife corridors while limiting future development on a key parcel along the Intracoastal Waterway. Read on to know more here:The estate, owned by a local family for decades, occupies a sprawling 42.57-acre site on the Clearwater Beach side of the Intracoastal, just south of the causeway that connects the barrier island to the mainland. In a region where most parcels have long been subdivided into condos, hotels and single-family homes, a holding of this size is exceptionally rare.The property includes a mix of developed and undeveloped land: a private residence, docks and outbuildings on a portion of the site, with the majority remaining as natural coastal habitat—mangrove forests, tidal wetlands, pine flatwoods and open meadows. That combination of location and natural character is what makes it both valuable to developers and attractive to conservationists.The family listed the estate for $37.5 million, positioning it as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for a buyer seeking privacy, water access and a large land bank in one of Florida’s most desirable coastal markets. At that price, the property is among the most expensive residential listings in the Clearwater area, reflecting not just the land’s size but also its waterfront position and development potential.For years, the owners have resisted pressure to sell or subdivide, preferring to keep the land intact. But as the family’s circumstances changed and the property’s maintenance costs grew, they decided to test the market, knowing that any sale would likely reshape this corner of Clearwater Beach.Almost as soon as the listing became widely known, state officials and conservation groups began looking at the property through a different lens. Caladesi Island State Park, which lies just across the Intracoastal from the estate, is one of the few remaining largely undeveloped barrier islands in the Tampa Bay region. The park protects beaches, dunes, mangroves and important nesting habitat for shorebirds and sea turtles.According to preliminary evaluations by the Florida Natural Areas Inventory (FNAI), the undeveloped portion of the Clearwater Beach estate, roughly 28 acres, contains high-quality natural communities that would significantly enhance the park if added to its boundaries. These include: mangrove forests and tidal creeks that serve as nurseries for fish and shellfish; coastal hammocks and pine flatwoods that provide habitat for native birds and small mammals; and buffer zones that help protect the park and neighbouring properties from storm surge and erosion.State agencies, including the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and Florida Forest Service, have begun exploring whether Florida Forever or other conservation funding programs could be used to acquire the land.Caladesi Island State Park is already a critical piece of the region’s conservation network, but it is surrounded by development on multiple sides. Adding the 28 acres from the Clearwater Beach estate would: expand the park’s footprint along the Intracoastal, creating a larger contiguous protected area; strengthen wildlife corridors that allow animals to move between habitats without crossing busy roads or developed zones; improve water quality by preserving mangroves and wetlands that filter runoff before it reaches the bay; and provide additional buffer against sea-level rise and stronger storms, which are increasingly threatening low-lying coastal parks.For conservation planners, the opportunity to add such a large, ecologically valuable parcel so close to an existing park is rare, especially in a heavily developed county like Pinellas.The owning family has not publicly committed to selling to the state, but representatives have indicated they are open to discussions that respect both their financial interests and the land’s conservation value. Any deal would need to balance the $37.5 million listing price against what the state can realistically pay using available conservation funds, which are often limited and competitive.Local reaction has been mixed. Some residents and business owners worry that a state acquisition could limit future economic development or reduce the tax base. Others, including environmental groups and many neighbours, see the potential park expansion as a once-in-a-generation chance to lock in open space and protect wildlife in an area that has seen intense development pressure.If the state moves forward, the purchase would likely be structured through Florida Forever, the state’s landmark conservation program that uses bond funding to acquire high-priority lands for parks, greenways and wildlife corridors. The FNAI preliminary evaluation, which rates properties based on their ecological significance and urgency, is often a key step in determining which lands qualify for such funding.Even if the state cannot acquire the entire 28-acre conservation target immediately, there are other possible arrangements, such as: purchasing the land in phases as funding becomes available; using conservation easements to protect the habitat while allowing limited private use on certain portions; and partnering with nonprofit land trusts to bridge funding gaps and manage the property.At its core, this situation is about more than one family’s estate or one park’s boundary. It’s about how Florida chooses to manage its remaining coastal wildlands in the face of rising property values, population growth and climate change.If the state succeeds in acquiring the 28 acres, Caladesi Island State Park will gain a significant expansion that could protect critical habitat for decades to come. If the land is sold for private development instead, the area will likely see new homes, docks and landscaping that fragment the habitat and reduce the ecological connectivity that conservationists value.For now, the 42.57-acre Clearwater Beach estate remains on the market, a large, green swath on maps that are otherwise crowded with rooftops and roads. Whether it becomes part of a state park or a new luxury enclave will depend on negotiations, funding and the choices made by a family that has guarded this land for generations.
Article Summary: A 42.57-acre family estate has sat on the market for $37.5 million. The state of Florida has expressed interest in acquiring roughly 28 acres of the property to expand Caladesi Island State Park. The potential deal would preserve mangroves, tidal creeks and wildlife corridors while limiting future development.

Article Title: US passport rules may change: Parents could need to prove citizenship status for children
Article Text:
Parents could be asked to provide a valid US passport or birth certificate to establish citizenship, or an I-94 form or permanent residency card to establish immigration status.

The US state department may require parents to provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status when applying for passports for their children. The latest draft is proposed amid US President Donald Trump's push to restrict birthright citizenship.According to a report by Reuters, the draft guidance outlines how the department could implement Trump’s August 6 executive order targeting so-called “birth tourism”. This targets foreign nationals travelling to the US to give birth so their children can obtain American citizenship. The proposal would require parents or legal guardians to submit documents proving their citizenship or immigration status as part of their child’s passport application.“The Department will require parental information and evidence of parental citizenship or immigration status as part of its determination ‌whether the ⁠applicant is subject to EO 14418,” the state department draft guidance reads, referring to the executive order.Under the proposed rules, parents could be asked to provide evidence such as a valid US passport or birth certificate to establish citizenship, or documents including an I-94 form or permanent residency card to establish immigration status.The information would be used to determine whether the child is eligible for US citizenship under the order.Currently, parents applying for a passport for a child born in the US are required to establish their relationship with the child and provide photo identification. Although the application asks whether a parent is a US citizen, supporting proof of the parent’s citizenship is not generally required as part of that process.The proposal comes as Trump intensifies his efforts to narrow the circumstances in which children born in the US can automatically acquire citizenship. His administration has argued that existing rules have encouraged birth tourism and other forms of what it considers abuse of the citizenship system.In a statement, state department spokesman Tommy Pigott said, “President Trump has been unequivocal that ​this administration will protect the meaning and value of American citizenship, full stop, and that includes making sure our passport adjudication process fully ​reflects that standard."Trump's first executive order on birthright citizenship sought to limit automatic citizenship to children born in the US who had at least one parent who was an American citizen or a lawful permanent resident, commonly known as a green card holder.The US Supreme Court later ruled that the order was unlawful, with a 6-3 majority finding that it violated the Citizenship Clause of the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution.Trump's August 6 order is narrower and specifically targets categories including children whose parents are foreign government employees, are allegedly involved in fraud or a commercial transaction to obtain citizenship, or are classified as an “alien enemy”. The order could still face legal challenges.Lawyers representing babies who could be denied citizenship under Trump's earlier order have already filed class-action lawsuits seeking to stop the administration's latest directive. One such case is before US District Judge Deborah Boardman in Greenbelt, Maryland.At a hearing on Friday, Boardman expressed scepticism about what she described as Trump's unprecedented order and allowed the plaintiffs to amend their lawsuit so that she could consider whether to block its implementation.Justice Department lawyers have argued that a restraining order would be inappropriate and that the legal challenge is premature because federal agencies had not yet issued public guidance on how the executive order would be enforced.
Article Summary: US state department may require parents to provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status when applying for passports for their children. The latest draft is proposed amid US President Donald Trump's push to restrict birthright citizenship. Parents could be asked to provide a valid US passport or birth certificate to establish citizenship, or an I-94 form or permanent residency card to establish immigration status.

Article Title: Pennsylvania police shooting: Officer charged in death of college student
Article Text:
A Pennsylvania police officer has been charged with voluntary manslaughter after shooting and killing a 22-year-old college student.

A Pennsylvania police officer has been charged with voluntary manslaughter after shooting and killing a 22-year-old college student who had wound up at the incorrect residence late at night while waiting for friends to pick him up, stated by the prosecutor on Tuesday.Upper Pottsgrove Police Cpl. Sean Farrell, 58, is accused of Glenwood Earl Pysher IV's death in August 23, according to Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin Steele. The officer did not have to kill Pysher during the confrontation since officer had less-lethal choices, according to the prosecuter.According to a news statement from the district attorney's office, the Montgomery County Detective Bureau looked into the shooting and examined video from Farrell's body-worn camera.According to the inquiry, "Cpl. Farrell had a taser and other less-lethal weapons on his utility belt that he did not use. The victim had his hands raised and was not carrying a weapon at the time of the shot, and the officer was safely behind a vehicle from Pysher. There was no danger from Mr. Pysher. This is not a legal use of deadly force, leading to the charge of Voluntary Manslaughter," as per the news release from Steele.Pysher's family lawyer thanked the prosecution in a statement.Attorney Ken Fulginiti stated, "The family is grateful for the work of the Montgomery County District Attorney's office and they are looking forward to justice in this horribly tragic, preventable, and reckless conduct that took their son's life."On Tuesday, Farrell surrendered to the Montgomery County Detectives. According to a district attorney's office representative, Farrell must surrender all firearms to the state police in order to be released after Magisterial District Judge Kathleen Rebar set bail at $75,000. On September 10, he will have a preliminary hearing.When a resident contacted 911 to report someone attempting to break into a home through the rear door, Farrell was the first officer on the scene. According to the statement, Farrell's body-worn video captured the officer moving down the driveway with his gun drawn and illuminating the path with its light.Farrell noticed Pysher on the patio of the house, close to the back door, while standing behind a car in the driveway. "Police, let me see your hands," shouted Farrell. "Hands up, hands up now, drop to the ground," he then shouted.According to the statement, Pysher was seen on camera raising his hands as he started to approach the officer and kept going in that way as the officer ordered, "Drop to the ground." "Drop to the ground," Farrell yelled once more, followed by "Stop or I'll..." However, according to the district attorney's office, Farrell fired two rounds before he could complete the sentence, striking Pysher twice in the chest.According to the announcement, Pysher was shot between 17 and 20 feet (5 and 6 meters) away from the officer.Pysher had been out at many pubs earlier in the evening to celebrate a friend's 21st birthday, according to the inquiry. Around 11 p.m., a designated driver took the party to the birthday person's house. About 30 minutes later, Pysher exited to walk half a mile to another friend's house to continue drinking, but he ended up at the incorrect residence, according to the release. Based on what his son's friends have told him, Pysher's father has stated that he thinks his son attempted to enter what he believed to be his friend's home.Glen Pysher told The Associated Press last week that "his son tried to open the doorknob and obviously startled the homeowner." According to what we know, he said, "He believed he was at his friend's house, so he said, "Hey! Open the door!"The father said that after his son sat down on the back porch and called his buddies, they noticed he was in the wrong area and started looking for him.Philip Stinson, a criminal justice professor at Bowling Green State University, maintains a national database of almost 25,000 police officer arrests since 2005.Stinson's research shows that between January 2005 and the end of July 2026, 218 local sworn police officers were charged with either murder or manslaughter in a fatal police shot that occurred while they were on duty. Although there are still a number of unresolved cases, 78 policemen have been found guilty, while 107 have been found not guilty or discharged.During that period, ten cops in Pennsylvania were accused, six of them were found guilty.According to Stinson, there have been variations in the number of cops charged over time, but those variations are statistically minor considering that there are about a thousand fatal police confrontations annually."These are ugly situations. "The facts are never simple," Stinson said. Criminal juries and grand juries appear to have similar problems. In a potentially violent street confrontation, they are hesitant to question the split-second, frequently life-or-death judgments made by an on-duty police officer.Most cops involved in deadly on-duty shootings shot an unarmed victim. Just ten of the victims in the 78 convictions had guns when they were shot.
Article Summary: Upper Pottsgrove Police Cpl. Sean Farrell, 58, is accused of Glenwood Earl Pysher IV's death in August 23, according to Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin Steele. Farrell had a taser and other less-lethal weapons on his utility belt that he did not use.

Article Title: In 1998, Jeopardy! host Alex Trebek donated 74 Hollywood Hills acres worth $2 million, nearly doubling local parkland and protecting trails and a wildlife corridor for deer and coyotes
Article Text:
The conservancy wanted it as a wildlife corridor where deer, coyotes and other animals could move between the Hollywood and San Diego freeways | Wikimedia Commons

Jeopardy!

The conservancy wanted it as a wildlife corridor where deer, coyotes and other animals could move between the Hollywood and San Diego freeways | Wikimedia Commons

Land next to Runyon Canyon
