A break from development

Alex Trebek is a game show host, most commonly known for. In 1998, he donated 74 acres of open land in the Hollywood Hills to the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy, with the property valued at $2 million at the time. The donation nearly doubled the public parkland in the area and protected land that officials wanted to preserve as a wildlife corridor.The property sits north of Hollywood Boulevard and east of Nichols Canyon Road, next to Wattles Park and Runyon Canyon Park. The land already had trails used by hikers and cyclists when Trebek made the donation, according to the Los Angeles Times.John Diaz was the acquisitions director for the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy at that time, who said that the agency planned to improve those trails after acquiring the property. The land had been sought for more than recreation, however since the conservancy wanted it as a wildlife corridor where deer, coyotes and other animals could move between the Hollywood and San Diego freeways.The land is now known as Trebek Open Space and is managed by the Mountains Recreation and Conservation Authority. The agency currently describes it as a 62-acre open space in the Hollywood Hills that adjoins Los Angeles' Runyon Canyon Park.Its existing network of fire roads is used as trails by hikers, mountain bikers and equestrians. The MRCA also identifies the property as land donated by Trebek.The difference between the original 74-acre figure and the current 62-acre description is a reflection of the way the property is documented today. The 1998 newspaper report described the entire parcel donated to the conservancy, while the MRCA's current park listing gives the size of the Trebek Open Space itself as 62 acres.The MRCA manages parks and open-space areas that preserve hillsides, canyons and wildlife habitat within the Los Angeles region. Trebek's property connects with other protected land around Runyon Canyon and Nichols Canyon, which gives hikers access to a landscape that is largely free of buildings despite its location near some of the city's busiest neighborhoods.Instead of treating the 74-acre donation as an isolated park, conservation officials incorporated it into the surrounding open-space network. Today, visitors can use the fire-road trails to move through the hills, while the undeveloped terrain provides cover and movement routes for wildlife living in the Santa Monica Mountains.The donation came at a time when undeveloped land in the Hollywood Hills was under pressure from development. Trebek transferred the property to the conservancy rather than retaining it, so it could remain open space.Trebek Open Space now sits beside Runyon Canyon Park, while its trails and surrounding hills form part of the network of open spaces across the Santa Monica Mountains. The MRCA has continued to maintain the property, and agency records show work at Trebek Open Space over the years, including hillside stabilization and vegetation management. For visitors, the property remains a trail area in the Hollywood Hills, and for the wildlife that moves through the surrounding mountains, the land remains undeveloped space between heavily built parts of Los Angeles.
Article Summary: In 1998, game show host Alex Trebek donated 74 acres of open land in the Hollywood Hills to the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy. The donation nearly doubled the public parkland in the area and protected land that officials wanted to preserve as a wildlife corridor. The land is now known as Trebek Open Space and is managed by the Mountains Recreation and Conservation Authority. Its existing network of fire roads is used as trails by hikers, mountain bikers and equestrians.

Article Title: In 2016, Clint and Maggie Eastwood donated 79 Carmel River acres for a $25 million flood-control project and public trail
Article Text:
The project was designed to give floodwater more room to spread across the former agricultural fields during major storms | Wikimedia Commons

The project was designed to give floodwater more room to spread across the former agricultural fields during major storms | Wikimedia Commons

It was the second Eastwood land donation

A floodplain that is designed to take stormwater

Wetlands and wildlife habitat

A trail connecting the coast and open space

Carmel River in the Ventana Wilderness | Wikimedia Commons

The project remains under development

Clint Eastwood and his former wife Maggie donated 79 acres of land along California's Carmel River to the Big Sur Land Trust in 2016. The land lies east of Highway 1 and south of the Carmel River Bridge, and became part of a planned $25 million project that aimed at restoring the river's floodplain, improving wildlife habitat and creating a public trail that links the coast with inland open space.In 1997, the Eastwoods had donated 49 acres of the Odello property to the Big Sur Land Trust, and the later 79-acre gift added another large section of the former agricultural land to the conservation project. Big Sur Land Trust's 2016 annual report said the donation at Odello East was a major step for what it called the Carmel River Floodplain Restoration and Environmental Enhancement, or Carmel River FREE, project. The organization's records described a planned 100-acre mosaic of restored habitats, which included wetlands, grasslands, willows and cottonwoods. The property had earlier been used for farming, and the restoration plan aimed at returning portions of the floodplain to a more natural state instead of keeping the river confined by its existing levees.The project was designed to give floodwater more room to spread across the former agricultural fields during major storms, and there were plans to remove nearly 1,500 feet of levee along the south side of the river and create multiple channels through the floodplain.The project also included replacing part of the Highway 1 embankment with a longer, taller bridge so water could move more freely between the floodplain and the Carmel Lagoon.Eastwood said floodwaters would be able to cross the property and reach the ocean instead of moving into nearby neighborhoods, when the donation was announced. KAZU reported that the project was intended to reduce the risk of another major flood like the one that affected the Carmel area in the mid-1990s.The project also aimed at restoring riparian and wetland habitat along the lower Carmel River and Carmel River Lagoon. Big Sur Land Trust's project documents said the restored areas would include native vegetation that could support steelhead trout, birds and other wildlife. A portion of the wider project area was also planned as an agricultural preserve, and the restoration would change how the former farm fields functioned during wet winters. The landscape would be changed completely so that water could occupy parts of the floodplain when river levels rose, instead of keeping stormwater away from the fields through engineered barriers.Once the project was completed, a trail was planned to run between Carmel River State Beach and Palo Corona Regional Park, and KAZU reported in 2016 that the trail would give visitors access to thousands of acres of open space. Big Sur Land Trust's annual report similarly described the trail as a connection between the coast and Palo Corona, alongside the habitat restoration work.The project therefore combined several uses for the same landscape, such as flood storage during major storms, wetland and river habitat, agricultural preservation and public recreation.The original 2016 announcement said the $25 million project was expected to be completed by 2020, but that deadline was not met. Big Sur Land Trust's current project page says Carmel River FREE is now in the final stages of design and pre-construction coordination, and also says that the project has about $25 million in grant funds and is awaiting a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant before construction can begin.The 128-acre project site now includes land donated by the Eastwoods as well as portions of Palo Corona Regional Park and Carmel River State Beach. The Eastwoods' 79-acre donation is still the largest privately contributed piece of the Odello East site and forms part of the land on which the floodplain restoration is planned.
Article Summary: Clint Eastwood and his former wife Maggie donated 79 acres of land along California's Carmel River to the Big Sur Land Trust in 2016. The land became part of a planned $25 million project that aimed at restoring the river's floodplain, improving wildlife habitat and creating a public trail. The property had earlier been used for farming, and the restoration plan aimed at returning portions of the floodplain to a more natural state.

Article Title: In 2008, a Texas couple bought an overgrazed ranch and removed its cattle; 19,300 restored acres later, its turkey population had climbed from fewer than 50 to more than 500
Article Text:
Representative image of wild turkeys thriving in a restored prairie habitat. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

A ranch gives its land a second chance

From overgrazed pasture to varied habitat

The ranch's turkey population increased from fewer than 50 birds to more than 500. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Why the turkey increase matters

In a landscape shaped for generations by cattle grazing, one Texas couple took a different approach to managing their newly acquired ranch. Instead of treating the land only as pasture, they began restoring its grasses, trees, water sources and wildlife habitat. Over time, the effort showed how land management can affect the species that depend on it.According to Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine , Mike and Mary Terry purchased an overgrazed property in 2008 and began restoring it to native grassland, eventually expanding their efforts across 19,300 acres. Within six months of acquiring the ranch, they sold their cattle to give the pastures time to recover. Cattle were reintroduced in 2015 under a more carefully managed grazing system.As the habitat improved, wildlife began returning to the property, including Rio Grande wild turkeys. The ranch's turkey population grew from fewer than 50 birds to more than 500, alongside improvements in grassland, tree cover and water sources. The recovery was not simply the result of removing cattle. Over the years, the Terrys combined periods of rest with controlled grazing, tree planting, water management and other habitat-restoration practices, creating conditions that allowed both the land and its wildlife to recover.After purchasing the ranch, the Terrys sold their cattle within months, giving heavily grazed pastures time to recover. Cattle were later reintroduced under a more carefully managed grazing system, alongside efforts to improve water sources and wildlife habitat. This approach is consistent with research published in the Journal of Wildlife Management , which examined habitat selection by Rio Grande wild turkeys in the Texas Panhandle and southwestern Kansas. The study found that turkeys selected areas with riparian vegetation, while females preferred nongrazed pastures for nesting at two study sites. It also found that light to moderate grazing followed by periods of rest did not reduce pasture use by male turkeys, suggesting that well-managed grazing can coexist with suitable turkey habitat.At MT7, restoration extended beyond grazing management. The Terrys planted trees including cedar elm, cottonwood and live oak, particularly around waterways, while more than 200 lakes and ponds have been maintained or created across the property. These changes have added vegetation, water and wetland habitat to the landscape, benefiting a range of wildlife. In addition to the ranch's growing Rio Grande wild turkey population, deer, quail, waterfowl, beavers and river otters have also been reported using the restored habitat. Together, the changes show how a working ranch can combine managed grazing with habitat restoration to create a more diverse landscape.Wild turkey populations can fluctuate with rainfall, food availability, nesting conditions and broader changes in the landscape. A study published by the Southeastern Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies found that male Rio Grande wild turkeys in South Texas used herbaceous and woody riparian habitats disproportionately during drought and were more likely to occur near supplemental resources such as water and food. The findings highlight how access to vegetation and water can become particularly important for turkeys when environmental conditions are difficult.The increase in turkeys at MT7 is part of a broader recovery of the ranch's habitat. Rather than removing cattle permanently, the Terrys incorporated grazing into a wider conservation strategy, using controlled grazing alongside vegetation management, tree planting and improvements to water resources. These efforts have helped create a landscape that supports both ranching and wildlife. The work was recognised in 2024, when Mike and Mary Terry received the Texas Leopold Conservation Award for their efforts to improve the health and productivity of their land while maintaining it as a working ranch.
Article Summary: Mike and Mary Terry purchased an overgrazed property in 2008 and began restoring it to native grassland. Within six months of acquiring the ranch, they sold their cattle to give the pastures time to recover. Cattle were reintroduced in 2015 under a more carefully managed grazing system. The ranch's turkey population grew from fewer than 50 birds to more than 500, alongside improvements in grassland, tree cover and water sources.

Article Title: In 2015, Paul Allen launched a global shark survey across 58 countries; cameras later found sharks missing from nearly 20% of reefs
Article Text:
PC: wikipedia

What did the underwater cameras reveal about reef sharks

Image AI generated

How can reef shark populations recover

How does shark loss affect coral reefs

In 2015, Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen launched Global FinPrint, a global survey that eventually deployed thousands of underwater cameras across coral reefs in 58 countries. The project was led by researchers at Florida International University and funded by the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, with more than 120 researchers across the western Atlantic, the Indian Ocean, the Western Pacific and the Central Pacific. In total, more than 400 reefs were surveyed across 58 countries and territories, producing over 20,000 hours of footage. The study published in Nature, titled ‘ Global status and conservation potential of reef sharks ’, showed that sharks were absent from nearly 20% of the reefs surveyed. The study linked this depletion to socio-economic factors including market proximity, poor governance, and population density, while also identifying shark sanctuaries, catch limits and marine protected areas as measures associated with higher shark abundance.Rather than using divers to conduct visual counts, the project relied on baited remote underwater video systems, or BRUVS According to Global FinPrint, researchers "usually set 30 to 100 BRUVS on a reef and record animal sightings for 60 minutes on each one."The research team drew on data from more than 15,000 standardised baited remote underwater video stations deployed on 371 reefs across 58 nations to estimate the global conservation status of reef sharks. Much of what was previously known about sharks had been inferred from industrial fishery catch records, with far less information available about sharks living in coastal habitats.The results reveal the profound impact of fishing on reef shark populations, with no sharks observed on almost 20% of the surveyed reefs. Reef sharks were found to be almost completely absent from reefs in several nations, and this depletion was strongly linked to socio-economic conditions, such as size and proximity of the nearest market, poor governance and human population density.The study's extended data further indicate that among the eight lowest-ranked nations surveyed, there was less than a 0.1% chance of a shark being present whenever a BRUVS was deployed, a level the authors describe as functional extinction. Functional extinction in this context means reef sharks are essentially absent from the ecosystem, with little to no functional role in structuring the surrounding reef fish community through predation or fear-based effects.Despite the scale of the declines, the study identifies opportunities for conservation. Shark sanctuaries, closed areas, catch limits and the absence of gillnets and longlines were all associated with substantially higher relative abundance of reef sharks, pointing to several policy pathways for restoring reef shark populations.As per Global FinPrint, reef sharks were largely absent in nations with high human population density and poor governance of marine resources; opportunities for conservation remain in most places. National shark fishing bans, fishing regulations and no-take marine protected areas are already being used successfully in different parts of the world to prevent reef shark extinctions, and the project also identified locations where reef sharks remain common enough to seed the recovery of populations elsewhere potentially.An estimated 100 million sharks are taken each year for their fins and meat, with many species suffering severe declines due to unregulated fishing. The organisation notes that shark fishermen in most nations use the whole animal fins, skins, cartilage, jaws and meat rather than practising "finning" alone, meaning that without careful controls, catches can exceed the ability of many shark species to replenish their populations. According to the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, one-quarter of sharks and their relatives are threatened with extinction. The loss of these predators, according to Global FinPrint, threatens the food security of nations that rely on fish for human consumption and threatens the dive tourism industry that relies on sharks as living attractions; while their absence can also disrupt the balance of marine food webs, causing large-scale habitat changes. Building on these findings, the next phase of research seeks to improve understanding of how sharks influence other reef animals, and how the loss of sharks could disrupt the balance of coral reefs, often described as the ‘rainforests of the sea’, around the world.
Article Summary: Global FinPrint deployed thousands of underwater cameras across coral reefs in 58 countries. In total, more than 400 reefs were surveyed across 58 countries and territories, producing over 20,000 hours of footage. Reef sharks were found to be almost completely absent from reefs in several nations. depletion was strongly linked to socio-economic conditions, such as size and proximity of the nearest market, poor governance and human population density.

Article Title: In 1995, Clint Eastwood sold a large California property for $3.08 million; the land was placed under permanent conservation protection instead of being developed
Article Text:
Clint Eastwood’s long connection to the land

The $3.08 million sale

The land was protected from future development

The property had been facing a very different future

The deal was linked to the fight over Odello Ranch

Eastwood later helped protect more coastal land

The financial side of the Malpaso deal drew scrutiny

Conservationists saw both benefits and complications

Malpaso Creek made the land environmentally significant

It was a sale rather than a celebrity land donation

A larger conservation legacy around Carmel

In 1995, actor and filmmaker Clint Eastwood sold roughly 280 acres of his California coastal property to Monterey County for $3.08 million, helping ensure that a large stretch of scenic land would remain undeveloped. The property, associated with Eastwood’s long-held Malpaso holdings near Carmel Highlands, was divided into five parcels and was acquired by the county for open-space preservation. Rather than becoming available for future construction, the land was placed under a conservation easement intended to protect it permanently. The transaction formed part of a wider conservation effort around Carmel and the Carmel River, where several important coastal properties were facing development pressure. Eastwood’s role in the episode was more complicated than a simple donation, since the county purchased the land, but the resulting protection prevented its future development.Eastwood began acquiring property around Malpaso Creek in the late 1960s, building a substantial collection of land along the rugged Monterey County coast. Contemporary accounts reported that his broader holdings in the area eventually covered roughly 650 acres, although the portion involved in the 1995 county transaction was considerably smaller.Eastwood had purchased land in the area during a period when development was increasingly changing parts of the Carmel region, while the coastal landscape around Malpaso Creek retained large areas of undeveloped terrain. The property’s location along Highway 1 and near the Big Sur coast also gave it considerable scenic and environmental importance.In 1995, Monterey County purchased approximately 279 to 280 acres of Eastwood’s Malpaso property for $3.08 million. The land consisted of five parcels and was acquired for open-space purposes. Contemporary reporting connected the transaction to California’s Proposition 70, a state bond measure that provided money for acquiring and protecting open space. The deal therefore involved a direct purchase rather than a straightforward charitable donation by Eastwood. The distinction matters because the conservation result came through a public acquisition in which the county became the owner of the property.One of the most significant aspects of the transaction was what happened after the county acquired the property. The Malpaso land was subject to a conservation easement that required its protection in perpetuity. The restriction was designed to prevent the county’s ownership from later being converted into a development opportunity. The arrangement meant that the property could remain open space rather than being subdivided or built over. Contemporary reporting also noted that the land was not simply turned into a conventional public park, with questions surrounding public access remaining separate from the permanent protection of the property itself.The significance of the acquisition becomes clearer when viewed against the development pressures affecting the Carmel area at the time. Nearby land around the Carmel River was also being considered for residential development, prompting conservation groups and local authorities to look for ways to preserve remaining open spaces. The Malpaso transaction became connected to a broader series of property deals involving the Eastwoods, Monterey County and the Big Sur Land Trust. Together, those efforts helped protect several hundred acres of environmentally and scenically important land around the Carmel coast.The 1995 Malpaso sale was particularly important because it was intertwined with the preservation of the nearby Odello Ranch, a former artichoke-growing property at the mouth of the Carmel River. Development plans had proposed dozens of homes on the approximately 134-acre property. The Eastwoods subsequently became involved in the complicated effort surrounding the site, purchasing the property after a development option was abandoned. The episode eventually helped lead to the preservation of much of the land rather than the residential development originally contemplated.The conservation story did not end with the Malpaso transaction. In 1997, Eastwood and Maggie Johnson announced an arrangement involving the transfer of substantial Coast Ranch land to the Big Sur Land Trust. Contemporary reports valued the property involved at about $6 million and said the arrangement would keep most of the land from being developed. The deal included restrictions affecting development rights and helped preserve open space around the Carmel River. The preservation effort also involved Monterey County land retained for flood-control purposes and agricultural protections on other portions of the property.The transaction was not without controversy. A later investigation by Coast Weekly examined the financial circumstances surrounding the Malpaso purchase and noted that Monterey County records had placed the property’s assessed value at about $308,682 in July 1994, far below the $3.08 million purchase price. That difference alone does not establish that the county overpaid, since a tax assessment is not necessarily the same as a property’s market value or its value for conservation purposes. However, the disparity became part of the scrutiny surrounding the transaction. The investigation also reported that county officials did not have a record of what Eastwood had originally paid for the property.The wider Eastwood land deals generated debate among conservationists and others involved in Monterey County land-use policy. Supporters pointed to the substantial amount of coastal and riverfront land that ultimately escaped development. Critics, meanwhile, questioned the financial and development-rights arrangements involved in the transactions, particularly around Odello Ranch. The debate illustrates that conservation victories involving private landowners and public authorities can involve complicated exchanges of property, development rights, water rights and tax considerations. Even with those disputes, the physical conservation outcome was significant because large areas that had faced development pressure were ultimately placed under long-term protection.The Malpaso property was valuable not only because of its dramatic coastal scenery but also because of its ecological setting. Malpaso Creek runs through the rugged Carmel Highlands landscape before reaching the Pacific, while the surrounding region contains important coastal habitats and Monterey pine forest. Monterey County planning documents have identified the Malpaso area as having significant conservation value, including its importance to Monterey pine habitat. Protecting undeveloped land in this landscape therefore helped preserve more than a scenic backdrop. It also maintained a relatively intact portion of a sensitive coastal environment where development could have fragmented habitat and altered the character of the landscape.The distinction between a sale and a donation is central to telling the story accurately. Eastwood did not simply give the roughly 280 acres to Monterey County for free. The county paid $3.08 million to acquire the five parcels, with Proposition 70 funding playing a role in the open-space acquisition. What makes the episode a conservation story is what happened through and after that purchase. The land was acquired for preservation and subjected to a permanent conservation restriction, removing the possibility of ordinary future development.The Malpaso transaction became one part of a broader pattern of land preservation associated with Eastwood’s property interests around Carmel. His involvement with the Mission Ranch, his earlier land transactions in Carmel Valley and the later preservation of land connected to Odello Ranch all contributed to a complicated local history in which privately held property was repeatedly at the centre of debates over development and conservation. The 1995 sale stands out because it converted roughly 280 acres of Eastwood’s coastal holdings into county-owned open space protected by a permanent conservation easement.The strongest legacy of the transaction is therefore not simply that a Hollywood star owned a large piece of California. It is that a substantial portion of his Malpaso property changed hands through a public conservation purchase at a time when development pressure was affecting the Carmel coast. Roughly 279 to 280 acres were sold for $3.08 million and placed under permanent conservation protection, ensuring that the land would not follow the conventional path from private ownership to subdivision and construction. The surrounding transactions were financially and politically complicated, but the central conservation outcome remains clear. A large area of environmentally and scenically important coastal land was secured as protected open space rather than developed.
Article Summary: Clint Eastwood sold 280 acres of his Malpaso property to Monterey County for $3.08 million in 1995. The land was acquired for open-space preservation and placed under a conservation easement. The transaction formed part of a wider conservation effort around Carmel and the Carmel River.

Article Title: Four California seniors reported scams in just 24 hours; police say cryptocurrency, gift-card and timeshare schemes cost them more than $315,000
Article Text:
The schemes involve cryptocurrency, timeshares and gift cards. (Representational AI photo)

4 scams, 24 hours

Police warn of pressure tactics

Helping seniors stay safe

Four seniors in Petaluma, California, have reported separate scams within just 24 hours, with suspected losses adding up to more than $315,000.The cases involved cryptocurrency, timeshares and gift cards. Petaluma police said officers responded to four separate reports from seniors who had been targeted through these schemes during the same period, Patch reported.The incidents have prompted police to warn residents to be careful when anyone asks them to send money. Officers said people should take time to check who is asking for the payment and whether the request is genuine before handing over money.The warning is particularly important for Petaluma, where people aged 65 and above make up more than 22% of the population, according to police. The department said this makes the community especially likely to see scams aimed at older residents.The four reports involved different types of scams, but they had one common element. Seniors were persuaded to give money through methods that were fraudulent.In one type of scheme, scammers used cryptocurrency. Cryptocurrency payments can be difficult to recover once they have been sent, making such demands particularly concerning for people who may not be familiar with digital currencies.Another reported scheme involved timeshares. Timeshare-related scams can involve requests for money connected to a property or an alleged transaction.Gift cards were also involved in one of the reported scams. Gift cards are sometimes used by scammers because they can ask victims to purchase cards and then share the card details or codes.Police said the suspected losses from all four incidents totalled more than $315,000. The department did not provide individual amounts for each case in its warning.The reports came within a short period, prompting Petaluma police to remind residents that scammers may try to create a sense of urgency.According to Petaluma police, scammers often tell people that their financial demands require immediate action. This pressure can make victims feel that they have to send money before they have time to check the request. Police warned that legitimate organisations will not pressure people to pay on the spot.Residents were advised to stop and check the request instead of acting immediately. Police said people should research the person or company involved and contact companies directly to confirm whether a payment request is genuine.The department also encouraged residents to speak to family members when they are unsure about a financial request. Asking another person for advice can give someone time to check whether the situation is legitimate before making a payment.Petaluma police said the department shares scam-prevention information online and also holds presentations in person. However, officers said residents also have a role to play in protecting older members of the community.The department urged people to check in with elderly neighbours and loved ones. Regular conversations can help families and neighbours identify suspicious requests and ensure that older residents do not become the next victims of a scam.
Article Summary: Four seniors in Petaluma, California, reported separate scams within 24 hours. The cases involved cryptocurrency, timeshares and gift cards. Police said the suspected losses from all four incidents totalled more than $315,000. The incidents have prompted police to warn residents to be careful when anyone asks them to send money.

Article Title: Tropical depression Edouard brings floods to Texas; knocks out power for thousands
Article Text:
Edouard was predicted to produce 3 to 7 inches (8 to 17 centimeters) of rain, with a maximum of 12 inches (30 centimeters), according to the hurricane center.

A storm hits the Texas-Louisiana border

Numerous storms in the Pacific

The former Tropical Storm Edouard deteriorated into a depression on Tuesday while delivering powerful gusts and heavy rains on portions of Texas, causing thousands of people to lose power, falling trees, and flooding highways.According to the National Hurricane Center , the storm reached Johnson Bayou, Louisiana, a tiny coastal town, with maximum sustained winds of 60 mph (95 kph). Forecasters predicted that it will continue to weaken until disappearing this week as it proceeded inland and passed across southeastern Texas.Meanwhile, a number of storms, including Lowell, which earlier in the day attained hurricane intensity, were building in the Pacific Ocean.Edouard was predicted to produce 3 to 7 inches (8 to 17 centimeters) of rain, with a maximum of 12 inches (30 centimeters), according to the hurricane center. Less was expected in southwestern Louisiana.Brad Reinhart, a senior hurricane expert at the National Hurricane Center stated, "that rainfall could produce some flash flooding and river flooding."The Texas Office of Emergency Management advised citizens to avoid the road when the storm's core moved over Beaumont, Texas, which is located approximately 80 miles (130 kilometers) northeast of Houston.The city's offices were closed.Beaumont Police said on social media that there were felled trees obstructing roadways, broken traffic lights, and flooded underpasses all around the city.According to the poweroutage.com report, around 32,000 utility customers in Jefferson county, which includes Beaumont, were without electricity.Mike Gilbert made the decision to close his surf store in Crystal Beach, Texas, ahead of the hurricane because he didn't want to put his staff at danger of having trouble returning home. However, he claimed that when Edouard made landfall around 60 miles (96 kilometers) northeast of his place on Tuesday, all that was left were gloomy sky and light rain.Gilbert said, "You literally never know." "It could have been a completely different story if it had suddenly moved over 50 miles and picked up 20 mph in the wind."Connor Salvador, the owner of an RV park along the ocean in Cameron, Louisiana, reported that by Tuesday morning, the gusts had increased and intermittent rain was falling. He stated that he wasn't too concerned about Edouard, even if there may be a "little bit" of flooding in case they receive a lot of rain.He remarked, "We're pretty used to all these types of storms that come through."According to forecasters, newly formed storm Lowell in the Pacific ocean is predicted to stay several hundred miles from Hawaii for the next several days at least. However, swells from the storm are expected to affect portions of the islands starting on Wednesday."This hurricane is likely to increase the surf and make for dangerous beach conditions and marine conditions for any boaters near the Hawaiian islands over the next few days", said by National Hurricane Center forecaster Andrew Hagan.Tropical Storm Marie developed in the Pacific Ocean early on Tuesday, well offshore of southwest Mexico as per the center.It was predicted by forecasters to develop into a hurricane by Wednesday night, and over the next several days, swells from the storm were also expected to impact portions of the coast in southwest Mexico and the Baja California peninsula.Driven by warm waters far from any land, Karina developed into a hurricane on Sunday in other parts of the Pacific. Forecasters stated on Tuesday that it was predicted to diminish after it intensified into a strong category 4 storm on Monday.The hurricane center reported that portions of Haiti, the Dominican Republic, the Turks and Caicos, and the Bahamas saw rain and thunderstorms due to the remnants of Tropical Storm Dolly.
Article Summary: Former Tropical Storm Edouard deteriorated into a depression on Tuesday while delivering powerful gusts and heavy rains on portions of Texas. Forecasters predicted that it will continue to weaken until disappearing this week as it proceeded inland and passed across southeastern Texas. A number of storms, including Lowell, which earlier in the day attained hurricane intensity, were building in the Pacific Ocean.

Article Title: Charlie Kirk murder case goes to trial; accused Tyler Robinson pleads 'not guilty' on all charges
Article Text:
Charlie Kirk murder case: Accused Tyler Robinson pled 'not guilty' to aggravated murder, six other charges

Tyler Robinson, the Utah man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including aggravated murder, after a judge ruled that the case can proceed to trial. Robinson could face the death penalty if convicted.Utah District Judge Tony Graf on Tuesday ruled that prosecutors had presented enough evidence to pursue the aggravated murder charge, siding with prosecutors who said they had a “mountain of evidence” against Robinson, 23.Prosecutors allege Robinson fatally shot Kirk while he was speaking to a crowd of more than 3,000 people at Utah Valley University in September 2025. Robinson turned himself in a day after the shooting.According to prosecutors, Robinson fired a high-powered, bolt-action rifle from a rooftop more than 400 feet (122 metres) away. They argue that he knew he could miss Kirk and strike someone else in the crowd. Prosecutor Ryan McBride said Robinson shot Kirk because he disagreed with his political views.The defence had sought to block the aggravated murder charge from going to trial or remove the possibility of the death penalty.Defence attorney Staci Visser argued that prosecutors had failed to establish the level of risk to others required under Utah law.“There was one shot. One bullet. One victim,” Visser argued, saying Kirk was elevated on a stage and was not immediately near others when he was shot in the neck.Prosecutor Chad Grunander countered that Robinson was armed with a bolt-action rifle loaded with additional rounds, arguing that he “came prepared to shoot again.”Graf nevertheless ruled that the aggravated murder charge could proceed, citing, among other factors, the positions of people in and around the tent where Kirk was speaking. A lesser murder charge would carry a minimum sentence of 15 years and a maximum of life in prison.During a five-day hearing in July, prosecutors presented DNA evidence they said linked Robinson to the rifle and to a tool allegedly used to engrave ammunition. Defence lawyers questioned the reliability of the DNA evidence.Prosecutors also presented a handwritten note they said Robinson left for his romantic partner before the shooting. The note allegedly said: “I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it.”Prosecutors are also seeking sentencing enhancements by alleging that Kirk was targeted because of his political beliefs. They cited an inscription on a bullet found in the rifle as evidence of a political motive, as well as a text message allegedly written by Robinson that said: “I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out.”The defence has disputed the evidence of a political motive.Kirk’s family welcomed the judge’s decision, calling it “an important step” in their pursuit of justice. His parents, Robert and Kathryn Kirk, attended the hearing at the heavily secured courthouse in Provo alongside his widow, Erika Kirk.A few dozen local members of Turning Point USA, the conservative youth organisation Kirk helped build, gathered outside the courthouse.Robinson showed little visible reaction during the hearing, while his mother cried.The case will now move towards trial, where prosecutors will have to prove the aggravated murder charge and the alleged political motive beyond a reasonable doubt.
Article Summary: Tyler Robinson, 23, is accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including aggravated murder. A judge ruled that the case can proceed to trial, siding with prosecutors. Robinson could face the death penalty if convicted.

Article Title: In 1993, Barbra Streisand gave her $15 million Malibu estate to conservation; the 24-acre property was planned as an environmental research centre
Article Text:
Barbra Streisand’s Ramirez Canyon property became a $15 million conservation gift

New conservation centre was planned for the heart of the Malibu estate

The property’s history stretched from political concerts to Art Deco interiors

The plan aimed to preserve the estate’s distinctive architecture and interiors

A major addition to the Santa Monica Mountains

For years, Barbra Streisand’s Ramirez Canyon estate had been a private Malibu retreat, complete with five houses, landscaped grounds and interiors reflecting her fascination with Art Deco.The property had proved difficult to sell, remaining on the market from 1987 until 1993, while its listing price fell from $18 million to $11.5 million. Then Streisand chose a very different future for the estate. According to Los Angeles Times, in November 1993, she agreed to donate the roughly 17,000-square-foot property to the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy, with state appraisers valuing the gift at $15 million. The plan went beyond simply protecting the land.The conservancy envisioned an environmental research centre, space for visiting scholars and researchers, conferences and eventual public access. For Streisand, the donation offered a way to keep the unusual estate together rather than see it gradually divided or lose the character that had made it distinctive.The Ramirez Canyon property was not an ordinary piece of undeveloped mountain land. Five houses stood across the estate, arranged among trees and gardens, with the buildings collectively covering roughly 17,000 square feet.For years, the property had also been on the real estate market.It was listed in 1987 and remained available until the summer of 1993. Its asking price had reportedly begun at $18 million before eventually falling to $11.5 million.By then, Streisand had started discussing another possibility with the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy. The conversations began around three months before the donation was announced.State appraisers valued the estate at $15 million, making it, according to the conservancy's executive director Joseph T. Edmiston, the most valuable property ever donated to the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area at that point, as reported by Los Angeles Times.The plan was not simply to preserve the estate as an untouched piece of Malibu. The conservancy intended to establish an environmental research complex there, called the Streisand Center for Conservancy Studies.The buildings were expected to provide space for environmental work, including a scholars-in-residence programme. Edmiston said the centre could accommodate visiting academics and researchers studying land conservation and related subjects.Part of the grounds was also expected to be opened to the public. The location offered a possible connection with the existing trail network through the Santa Monica Mountains, giving the property a role beyond research and administration.The conservancy was due to take possession on December 1, 1993. Its first planned conference was scheduled for February and was to focus on greenways including former rights of way, railway routes and other corridors that could be incorporated into urban park systems.The estate had already played a public role before its donation. In 1986, Streisand hosted a benefit concert there for Democratic senatorial candidates. The event was taped for cable television and marked her first public performance in six years.Reportedly, the concert raised $1.5 million for the political candidates. The televised programme also generated an estimated $7 million for charities and causes supported by Streisand.Away from the concert, the property was known for its collection of distinctive houses and its carefully designed interiors. One of the residences was featured in Architectural Digest in late 1993, with particular attention given to Streisand's interest in Art Deco design.That house contained an extensive collection of period furniture and decorative objects. Much of the collection was due to be offered at auction in New York the following March.The estate's buildings were not expected to disappear simply because the land was moving into conservation ownership. Edmiston described the collection of structures as part of what made the property suitable for the proposed centre.There was an English country-estate quality to the grounds, alongside several different architectural styles. Two of the houses had a country character, with one resembling a heavily remodelled barn. Another was a Mediterranean-style villa with a projection room measuring about 2,000 square feet.The conservancy was also interested in retaining some of the furnishings. Rather than stripping the buildings of their interiors, officials hoped Streisand might donate at least part of the Art Deco collection as well. If that was not possible, they considered purchasing selected pieces.Edmiston said, “There have been three major donations in the history of the Santa Monica Mountains”.The Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy had been established in 1981, with responsibilities that included acquiring land in the mountains and supporting environmental education. By the time of Streisand's gift, it had acquired about 20,000 acres.The organisation placed the new donation alongside two earlier major private gifts. The first was the 186-acre Will Rogers estate, which entered the state park system in 1944. At the time, that property had been valued at $550,000.The other was the 10-acre oceanfront estate of actor Leo Carrillo, donated later and valued at $300,000.Streisand's property was considerably larger in both its appraised value and the scale of its buildings. Its intended use also reflected the conservancy's expanding interest in research and environmental education.
Article Summary: Barbra Streisand donated her Malibu estate to the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy in 1993. The plan was to establish an environmental research complex there. The gift was valued at $15 million, making it the most valuable property ever donated to the mountains.

Article Title: Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi get slight relief as Pak HC bars solitary confinement
Article Text:
Pak HC intervenes over Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi's detention, bars solitary confinement

A Pakistan high court on Tuesday directed authorities at Rawalpindi Jail to ensure that former prime minister Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi are not held in solitary confinement. The ruling also set out provisions for Khan's family meetings, phone calls, reading material and medical care.The Islamabad High Court (IHC), while hearing petitions challenging the couple's alleged solitary confinement, directed the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules and arrange telephone conversations with his sons.Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro also ordered the jail to provide Khan with newspapers and books every day and ensure access to medical facilities as prescribed under jail rules. Rawalpindi's Aiala jail superintendent has been asked to implement the directions and submit a compliance report within 15 days, according to the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The court had earlier reserved its verdict on August 6 on separate petitions filed by Khan's sister Aleema Khanum and Bushra Bibi's daughter Mubashra Khawar Maneka. The IHC also held the petitions challenging the alleged solitary confinement to be maintainable.The 73-year-old cricketer-turned-politician and his wife have been in custody since August 2023 and is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. Khan's Tehreek-e-Insaf party and supporters have maintained that the cases are politically motivated, while the government has rejected allegations of mistreatment.Bushra Bibi was first jailed in January 2024 after being convicted in a corruption-related case. She was released on bail in October that year after nearly nine months in custody but was arrested again in January 2025 following another corruption conviction. She remains at Adiala Jail.The IHC order comes as Khan's detention and medical treatment remain the subject of separate proceedings before the Supreme Court.On Monday, the Supreme Court declined an application by Khan's sister Uzma Khan seeking an early hearing of her contempt petition against government officials over the alleged failure to comply with an earlier order concerning his transfer to a private hospital, Dawn reported.Pakistan's Supreme Court had on August 18 ordered that Khan be shifted to the privately run Shifa International Hospital after concerns were raised by his family and supporters over his health, including an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year.Instead, Khan was taken to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on the night of August 20-21 for a medical procedure and diagnostic examinations and was later returned to Adiala Jail.Uzma Khan's petition contends that this breached the Supreme Court's direction that Khan remain admitted at the Islamabad hospital until the next hearing on September 16. The government has defended the decision, citing security concerns.Two specialists from Shifa International Hospital also participated in Khan's eye examination at PIMS, according to the hospital administration, as reported by Dawn.Uzma Khan had sought an earlier hearing, arguing that further delay could affect the enforcement of the Supreme Court's order. The Supreme Court, however, rejected the request under its case-fixation policy, noting that 94 other criminal original petitions in the same category were pending, Dawn reported.The contempt petition is listed for September 16 before a three-member bench comprising Justices Shahid Waheed, Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Ishtiaq Ibrahim. The bench is also scheduled to hear other matters concerning Khan's health and family meetings.
Article Summary: Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi have been in custody since August 2023. The couple is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. The Islamabad High Court ordered the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules.

Article Title: Pakistan court allows Hindu woman to return home after alleged forced conversion, marriage

Woman returns from Pakistan

He alleged that CCTV footage showed unidentified people taking Reeta from the family home along with valuables and mobile phones on August 24.According to the complaint, Reeta was taken to Gujranwala in Punjab, some 80 kms from Lahore, where she was allegedly pressured to convert to Islam and marry Nazeer Hussain, who was already married.Punjab Police later recovered Reeta and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday. Article Title: Watch: 'Driverless' car crashes into police van after internet outage in Islamabad
Article Text:
In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work and warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.

A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration, with footage of the incident going viral and sparking a wave of memes online.According to local media, the incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital, where journalist Muhammad Aalijah was recording a video of a technology-based automated-driving system developed by Abbottabad-based technology enthusiast Ehsan Zafar. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction.Footage shared by Aalijah shows him sitting in the front passenger seat as he explains the vehicle's features while it moves along the road. The remotely controlled steering wheel then appears to lose control, sending the car towards a police van parked nearby.Aalijah can be seen attempting to stop the vehicle by pulling the handbrake, but the car continues moving and bumps into the police vehicle.Aalijah later told Dawn that he had been asked by Zafar to report on his technology-based automated-driving innovation. He attributed the crash to a "technical fault" triggered by an internet disruption.“Everything was fine until a technical fault occurred due to an internet disruption, causing the car to go out of control and crash into a police vehicle,” he said.According to Aalijah, the vehicle was operated remotely through internet and satellite connections. The loss of the internet connection during the demonstration caused the car to become uncontrollable.In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work.“The sole purpose was to raise awareness and urge people to remain cautious until any new experiment or technology has been thoroughly tested, proven safe and established as a complete success,” he said.“This was a message of caution, not an attempt to discredit anyone.”Aalijah also warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.“The vehicle was being operated through satellite and internet connections, but during external control, it went out of control as soon as the internet connection was disconnected and collided with a police vehicle,” he wrote.He said the relatively low traffic at D-Chowk limited the potential consequences of the malfunction, but warned that a similar failure on a busy road could have been far more serious.“If the same situation had occurred on a busy road, the consequences could have been extremely dangerous, even fatal,” he said.“This video is not criticism; it is a responsible effort to raise awareness and issue a warning by all means, experiment, but ensure safety first,” he added.
Article Summary: A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration. The incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction. Footage of the incident went viral and sparked a wave of memes online.

Article Title: Pak PM scrambles for damage control after his office edits leaders out of SCO summit photo

opportunities, while stressing dialogue and diplomacy as the way forward in addressing conflicts.
